poems.title: Saturday Garage
poems.body:
The garage door groans up like morning,
and dust goes gold in the one bright beam.
Wrenches lined by size, not sentiment,
though sentiment is why they're clean.

You hand me tools before I ask.
I hand you nothing back but time —
the kind that doesn't rush the bolt,
the kind that fathers learn to find.

Radio low. Coffee going cold.
Some engine ticking as it cools.
We are not fixing much of anything.
We are just here, among the tools.

comments.name: A reader
comments.text: The last stanza got me. That is exactly what those Saturdays felt like.

poems.title: What the Maple Knows
poems.body:
Every year it lets go first —
red before the others blush,
brave or simply tired, who's to say,
of holding on so hard, so hushed.

I used to think that losing leaves
was something like defeat.
Now I watch the maple empty out
and call the emptying complete.

Bare branches hold the winter sky
the way a hand holds nothing well —
open, waiting, unashamed,
with a story it won't tell.

poems.title: Ode to a Kitchen Table
poems.body:
Fifty years and you have not complained,
you patient acre of scarred and honest oak.
You held the homework and the hospital forms,
the birthday candles, the bad news gently spoke.

You wear your history where we can read it:
that ring from a glass nobody thought to lift,
the gouge my brother swears he didn't make,
the worn pale places — every one a gift.

Other furniture gets replaced. Not you.
You are the argument for staying put,
for being the flat and steady thing
a family sets its elbows and its supper on.

Bless your four plain legs. Bless your dull shine.
Bless the way you never once gave way
under all the weight we asked you to hold —
and held, and hold, and will hold, day by day.

comments.name: M.
comments.text: I can picture the exact table. The gouge line made me laugh out loud.

poems.title: Growing Room
poems.body:
We moved your bed to make you room
though you were barely gone.
I stood there with a screwdriver
not knowing what came on

so strong it stopped my hands —
just a bed frame, just a wall,
just a kid who isn't little,
who was never little at all,

not really, not the way I kept it
folded in my chest.
The room got bigger. So did you.
I am still doing my best

to let the small rooms go.

poems.title: Ode to the Coffee Cup Left Out All Night
poems.body:
Faithful ring on the windowsill,
you kept your inch of cold black tide
through all the hours I was asleep
and never once complained, or dried.

You are not beautiful. You chipped
in ninety-eight and stayed. You hold
what I abandoned, and you hold it
the way the patient hold the old.

Small brown moon, low and steady,
first thing my hand finds in the gray —
teach me your trick of simply waiting
for someone to come back your way.

poems.title: Late August
poems.body:
The light comes in low and gold now,
tired of standing straight up all summer.
Cicadas wind down like a clock
nobody remembered to keep wound.

I mow the last of the long grass
and the smell of it says something
I don't have better words for —
green, and going, and good.

Soon the maple will start its argument
with the sky. Soon the mornings
will ask for a jacket. But tonight
the porch light is enough. The bugs
know it. I do too.

comments.name: A reader
comments.text: "tired of standing straight up all summer" — stealing that line for how I feel too.
